questions.question: Describe South Africa's three-part topography and classify slopes by shape, explaining why this national structure makes slopes central to South African geography.
questions.expected_answer: The country divides into three structural units. The interior plateau is a high ancient erosion surface mostly between 1 200 and 1 800 metres, carrying the Highveld, the Free State plains and the Karoo basin. Around it runs the Great Escarpment, the nearly continuous rim where the plateau breaks toward the sea — highest in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg above 3 000 metres, continuing as the Nuweveld and Roggeveld rims and the escarpment edges of Mpumalanga and Limpopo. Between escarpment and sea lies the marginal zone: the folded Cape ranges, stepped terrace country and the humid east-coast lowlands. This build makes slopes central: the plateau gives gentle surfaces, the escarpment gives the steepest slopes in the country — one to two vertical kilometres in a few horizontal ones — and the marginal zone is the staircase between, so rivers leaving the plateau plunge over falls like the Tugela's nearly 950-metre drop, and roads climb through passes. Slopes classify by shape: convex bulges outward and steepens downhill; concave hollows inward, gentlest at the base; rectilinear holds one constant angle; compound slopes stack several shapes downhill, as most real hillsides do.

questions.question: Name and characterise the four slope elements in order, and explain slope retreat, contrasting parallel retreat with slope decline and stating why South African conditions favour retreat.
questions.expected_answer: From summit to plain: the crest, gently convex, thinly covered, slowly rounded by weathering; the cliff or free face, the steepest element, near-vertical bare bedrock wherever a resistant band outcrops — called the free face because loosened rock falls away at once, keeping it sheer; the talus or debris slope, rectilinear because loose fragments settle at their angle of repose of roughly 25 to 35 degrees, with coarse blocks high and fines low — a slope of transport; and the pediment, a gently concave bedrock surface under about 5 degrees with a thin sediment veneer, swept by sheetwash and merging with the plain. A soft-rock hill without a resistant band lacks cliff and talus. Slope retreat is the machine in motion: the cliff sheds rock and is rebuilt further back, the talus follows, and the pediment grows forward. In Lester King's parallel retreat, developed on South African landscapes, the profile keeps its proportions as it relocates backward; over deep time opposing slopes consume uplands, pediments merge into pediplains, and koppies and inselbergs survive as remnants. The rival model, slope decline, has the whole profile lowering and rounding with age — typical of humid, deep-soiled regions. South Africa's semi-arid climate, resistant caprocks and sparse vegetation favour parallel retreat, which is why local landscapes keep sharp profiles for tens of millions of years.

questions.question: Explain spatial and spectral resolution, the vector data types with attribute data, and the raster model, and show how a GIS applies these to slope studies.
questions.expected_answer: Spatial resolution is the ground area one pixel represents: at 30 metres fields, dams and roads register but vehicles vanish; at 10 metres farm tracks appear — finer resolution, smaller detail. Spectral resolution is the number and narrowness of wavelength bands a sensor records — visible, near-infrared, thermal — and because every surface reflects the bands in its own signature, more and narrower bands separate healthy veld from stressed crops, bare soil from water. Vector data stores the world as geometry: points for single-position features like a windpump or beacon; lines for rivers, roads and contours; areas or polygons for farms, reservoirs or districts; with attribute data — the table of facts such as depth, surface type or rainfall — attached to each object. Raster data spreads a grid of equal cells over the land with one value per cell, as in a digital elevation model or a satellite band, and suits continuously varying phenomena like altitude and rainfall, while vector suits discrete objects with edges. Applied to slopes: a raster digital elevation model yields a slope-angle map of a whole district at one command, vector contours, rivers and boundaries overlay it, and combining slope, soil and rainfall layers flags hillsides too steep to cultivate, gully-prone pediments and cuttings needing inspection — the working method of conservation planners and municipal engineers.
